PHBR1 p.107. Wearing no head protection costs NOTHING in Vision or Hearing -- but under the optional hit location rules an attacker may make a Called Shot at the head and thereby IGNORE the character's AC benefits from armor. Bonuses from shields, high Dexterity and magical items still count. At a total -8 to hit this is rarely worth it unless the victim is otherwise heavily armored -- which is exactly when it is worth it. NOTE that head protection does NOT change Armor Class: a warrior in full plate has the same AC with a great helm, with no helmet at all, or anything between.

Close-fitting helmet with visor PHBR1 p.106/108 names the basinet as its example of the CLOSED-FACE HELMET: metal, like the open-faced helmet except that there is armor plate, often a visor which may be opened, in front of the face. -2 Vision, -3 Hearing. The galea worn by gladiators and the myrmillo are also of this type, as are the helmets of many knights and mounted warriors. BENEFIT: if the wearer is also in plate mail or field plate, he gets +1 to saving throws vs. dragon breath and vs. fire-based spells and magical effects such as burning hands, pyrotechnics, fire ball, flaming sphere, wall of fire, delayed blast fireball, incendiary cloud and meteor swarm, as determined by the DM. HINDRANCE: if a lasso, chain or bolas is used to snare the head of a rider wearing one, he rolls 1d6 -- on 4-6 the attack is handled normally, but on 1-3 it is treated as a normal lasso or chain dismount and the attacker does NOT get the extra damage a head-lasso normally allows.

Full face coverage, -1 to initiative, limits vision PHBR1 p.106/108: a massive helm covering the entire head from the top of the head to the top of the shoulders, leaving slits open for the eyes and holes open for breathing; it has NO removable visor. -3 Vision, -4 Hearing, the worst of the six types. BENEFITS: +2 to saving throws vs. wizard spells such as hypnotism, light cast on his eyes, blindness, hypnotic pattern, suggestion, fire charm, rainbow pattern and other mind-controlling spells -- but NOT charm person, charm monster or domination. If the wearer is also in plate mail or field plate he gets +2 to saving throws vs. dragon breath and vs. fire-based spells and effects.

Soft leather cap, minimal protection PHBR1 p.106/108 calls this the CAP: a padded, leather or even steel skullcap about the size of and worn much like a close-fitting cap, beret or hat. No Vision penalty and only -1 to Hearing, as it partially covers the ears. Often worn in conjunction with padded, leather, hide, studded leather and other lightweight armors. WEIGHT DISCREPANCY: PHBR1 p.106 gives 2 lb; the previous unsourced value here was 1 lb. PHBR1's is adopted, being the only sourced figure available.

Standard metal helmet, protects against critical hits (optional rule) PHBR1 p.106/108 calls this the OPEN-FACED HELMET: reinforced leather or metal covering the back, sides and top of the face, leaving most of the face open. -1 Vision, -2 Hearing (it completely covers the ears, usually with small holes or grating so the wearer can hear at all). Corinthian helmets of ancient Greece are the example; in a medieval campaign these are often worn by military officers and soldiers who can afford the protection. WEIGHT DISCREPANCY: PHBR1 p.106 gives 5 lb; the previous unsourced value here was 10 lb. PHBR1's is adopted, being the only sourced figure available.

Quilted cloth helmet PHBR1 p.106/108 calls this the COIF: a padded chain mail hood fitting snugly around the neck and over all the head except the face from chin to forehead. No Vision penalty, -1 to Hearing. Usually worn with chain mail. A heavily armored knight often wears a coif AND a Great Helm over it; the only benefit that confers is that he can remove the Great Helm to see and hear better while still having some head protection. WEIGHT DISCREPANCY: PHBR1 p.106 gives 2 lb; the previous unsourced value here was 1 lb. PHBR1's is adopted, being the only sourced figure available.

Magical elven-made chain, lighter and quieter. Usable by wizards and thieves.

PHBR2 p.93. Elfin chain with EACH INDIVIDUAL LINK WRAPPED in thin leather or light cloth binding, which to some extent silences the armor. AC, movement and the magical nature are elfin chain's; only weight, cost and the thief-skill column differ. WEIGHT IS THE PROSE RULE, NOT TABLE 31. p.93 sets encumbrance at ONE-THIRD ABOVE normal elfin chain, which at elfin chain's canon 15 lb gives 20 lb. TABLE 31 (p.103) PRINTS 50 lb AND IS AN ERROR -- 50 lb is plate mail's exact weight, and the same sentence benchmarks the COST against plate mail, so the compiler appears to have carried the wrong figure across. Chris's ruling, August 2026. A relative rule also survives any later correction to elfin chain's weight, which a flat 50 would not. COST: Table 31 gives 750 gp and up, legality S, and marks it hard to obtain. That sits above plate mail's 600 gp exactly as the prose requires ("fiendishly expensive, costing more than plate mail"). NOTE THE FRICTION with the Elven Chain Mail record's unattributed 5000+ gp: PHBR2 plainly is not working from that baseline, and on these numbers the rarer item is the cheaper one. Not resolved here. RARER THAN ORDINARY ELFIN CHAIN. Finding a craftsman and persuading him to make a suit could be an adventure in itself. TABLE 28 -- EFFECT ON THIEF SKILLS: Pick Pockets -25, Open Locks -5, Find/Remove Traps -5, Move Silently 0, Hide in Shadows -10, Detect Noise 0, Climb Walls -25, Read Languages 0. THE DASHES IN THAT TABLE ARE ZEROES, NOT OMISSIONS, and reading them so is what makes the prose beneath it true: against ordinary elfin chain (Table 38: -20/-5/-5/-10/-10/-5/-20/0) this is 10 BETTER at Move Silently and 5 BETTER at Detect Noise, paid for by 5 WORSE at Pick Pockets and Climb Walls. The book's "bonuses ... above those which apply for normal elfin chain" are therefore relative, not absolute -- the table shows no positive number anywhere. Useful to a thief who needs to sneak but expects to fight.

PHBR1 pp.105-106. A pair of armored sleeves, an oriental form of armor unknown in the west, which may be worn concealed under the samurai's tunic. Costs TWICE as much as a buckler and acts almost the same. THE FACT THAT KOTE COME AS A PAIR DOES NOT MEAN +2 TO AC -- only the +1 a buckler normally confers. Two differences from a buckler: kote CANNOT BE DISARMED, and the wearer can still use weapons in both hands. Its Dexterity-check penalty is the buckler's, counted only for Juggling, Tightrope Walking and Tumbling.
